newsitem.title: USA: Healthdyne keeps control in takeover battle.
newsitem.headline: Healthdyne keeps control in takeover battle.

text.p: Medical device company Healthdyne Technologies Inc. retained the upper hand Wednesday in a six-month fight for control of the company as shareholders re-elected its board of directors and rejected a dissident slate offered by hostile bidder Invacare Corp..

Although the final tally will not be released for at least several days, Healthdyne Chairman Parker Petit said preliminary results indicate that shareholders overwhlemingly re-elected the seven-member board.
Invacare, a medical equipment company which has launched a $200 million hostile bid for Healthdyne, had submitted a four-man slate to take majority control of the board.

"We are grateful that shareholders have shown support for the company's nominees and recognised that Invacare's proposal for a split board and 'fire sale' of the company would only have produced deadlock, controversy, delay and expense and would have been detrimental to the company and its shareholders," Petit said in a news release.

However, Healthdyne also said it appeared that shareholders had approved several proposals submitted by Invacare, including one that sets a 10 percent threshhold for shareholders to call a special meeting. Healthdyne's current rules allow shareholders owning 60 percent of the company to call a special meeting, although Healthdyne had promised to cut that to 25 percent.

At an hourlong annual meeting attended by Invacare's key officers as well as about 120 Healthdyne shareholders and employees, Healthdyne attacked Invacare's offer and its methods. Healthdyne has rejected the $15-per-share offer as grossly inadequate.

"Mr. Mixon ought to tend to his own business for a while," Petit said, referring to Invacare Chief Executive Malachi Mixon. Petit noted that Invacare's financial position recently has declined while Healthdyne's business has topped Wall Street's expectations.

Petit also stressed that the company will continue to pursue talks with other potential suitors and speculated that more buyers may emerge now that the proxy fight is over. Healthdyne has said an unidentified party has expressed interest at buying the company for more than $15 per share.

"Having this process over will allow us to move down the road," he said at a news conference after the meeting. He did not set any time frame for a potential transaction, but said it would likely move forward in "weeks, not months."

Meanwhile, Mixon said Invacare intends to pursue its takeover efforts with an appeal of a court decision that upheld part of Healthdyne's anti-takeover plan known as a "poison pill." He also said Invacare has not yet determined whether it will extend its hostile tender offer, which is set to expire Aug. 1.

"I think it was a pretty good day. We came in as underdogs. We didn't really expect to win the directors (vote)," Mixon said at a news conference after the meeting, adding that he believed the directors vote was closer than Petit had indicated.
Invacare also plans to keep close watch for any potential suitors of Healthdyne. Invacare repeatedly has expressed scepticism about the appearance of a "white knight" for Healthdyne.

"Mr. Petit has promised Wall Street he has another buyer at a substantially higher price. We don't believe it. If he does have another buyer, so be it. We'll still be around. We'll be observing, watching, waiting," Mixon said.
Mixon also noted that Invacare or other investors could potentially seek to call a special shareholder session if a transaction does not materialise.
Healthdyne slipped 6 cents to $16.625 in consolidated late afternoon trading on the New York Stock Exchange, while Invacare dropped 62.5 cents to $22.75 on Nasdaq.
